content: 1. Zidovudine can increase the toxicity of amphotericin B deoxycholate through pharmacodynamic synergism. This interaction is considered minor, but its clinical significance is unknown. Close monitoring is recommended. 2. Atazanavir and zidovudine both elevate the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Caution should be exercised, and patients should be closely monitored. 3. Zidovudine and atidarsagene autotemcel should not be used together. Antiretroviral therapies (ARTs) may interfere with the manufacturing of atidarsagene autotemcel. ARTs should be discontinued for at least one month before cell mobilization or until the medications are fully eliminated. 4. Azathioprine and zidovudine can mutually increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, leading to an elevated risk of myelosuppression. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 5. Zidovudine and betibeglogene autotemcel should not be co-administered. ARTs should be stopped at least one month before mobilization and until all apheresis cycles are completed, as they may interfere with the manufacturing of apheresis-derived cells. 6. Black cohosh can increase the toxicity of zidovudine through pharmacodynamic synergism, potentially raising the risk of hepatotoxicity. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown, but close monitoring is recommended. 7. Carboplatin and zidovudine can increase each other’s toxicity via pharmacodynamic synergism, heightening the risk of myelosuppression. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 8. Cidofovir and zidovudine can increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism. When cidofovir is administered with probenecid, zidovudine clearance may decrease. The zidovudine dose should be reduced by 50% on days of cidofovir/probenecid administration. Close monitoring is essential. 9. Cisplatin and zidovudine can mutually enhance toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, increasing the risk of myelosuppression. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 10. Clarithromycin may increase or decrease zidovudine levels through an unknown mechanism. Conflicting reports exist in the literature. Administration should be separated by 2 to 4 hours, and close monitoring is recommended. 11. Clofarabine and zidovudine can increase each other’s toxicity via pharmacodynamic synergism, raising the risk of myelosuppression. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 12. Clozapine and zidovudine can mutually increase toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, significantly elevating the risk of myelosuppression. Alternative drugs should be considered. 13. Conivaptan can increase zidovudine levels by affecting hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 14. Zidovudine can decrease cyanocobalamin levels through an unspecified interaction mechanism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 15. Zidovudine and dapsone can increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, potentially leading to increased bone marrow toxicity. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown, but close monitoring is recommended. 16. Dasatinib and zidovudine can mutually enhance toxicity via pharmacodynamic synergism, increasing the risk of myelosuppression. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 17. Deferiprone and zidovudine can increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism. This combination should be avoided or alternative drugs used. If unavoidable, absolute neutrophil counts should be monitored more frequently. 18. Dexrazoxane and zidovudine can increase each other’s toxicity via pharmacodynamic synergism, heightening the risk of myelosuppression. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 19. Zidovudine can increase didanosine levels by decreasing renal clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 20. Doxorubicin can decrease the effects of zidovudine, while zidovudine can increase the toxicity of doxorubicin through pharmacodynamic synergism. This interaction raises the risk of myelosuppression. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 21. Doxorubicin liposomal can decrease the effects of zidovudine, while zidovudine can increase the toxicity of doxorubicin liposomal through pharmacodynamic synergism. This interaction also increases the risk of myelosuppression. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 22. Efavirenz and zidovudine both elevate the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 23. Zidovudine and elivaldogene autotemcel should not be co-administered. ARTs should be discontinued for at least one month before initiating stem cell mobilization medications and until all apheresis cycles are completed. 24. Elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir DF is a complete HIV regimen and should not be administered with zidovudine or other antiretrovirals. 25. Emtricitabine and zidovudine both increase the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 26. Enfuvirtide and zidovudine both elevate the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 27. Fluconazole can increase zidovudine levels by decreasing its metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 28. Zidovudine can increase the toxicity of flucytosine through pharmacodynamic synergism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 29. Food can decrease zidovudine levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral form of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 30. Fosamprenavir and zidovudine both increase the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 31. Ganciclovir can increase zidovudine toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism. This combination is contraindicated. 32. Hydroxyurea and zidovudine can increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, raising the risk of myelosuppression. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 33. Ibritumomab tiuxetan and zidovudine can mutually enhance toxicity via pharmacodynamic synergism, increasing the risk of myelosuppression. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 34. Ifosfamide and zidovudine can increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, heightening the risk of myelosuppression. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 35. Imatinib and zidovudine can mutually enhance toxicity via pharmacodynamic synergism, increasing the risk of myelosuppression. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 36. Indinavir and zidovudine both elevate the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 37. Interferon alfa-2b can increase zidovudine levels by decreasing its metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 38. Interferon alfa-n3 can increase zidovudine levels by decreasing its metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 39. Interferon beta-1a can increase zidovudine levels by decreasing renal clearance. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 40. Interferon beta-1b can increase zidovudine levels by decreasing renal clearance. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 41. Kava can increase zidovudine toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, potentially raising the risk of hepatotoxicity. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 42. Ketoconazole can increase zidovudine levels by affecting hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 43. Lamivudine and zidovudine both elevate the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 44. Lenalidomide and zidovudine can increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, heightening the risk of myelosuppression. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 45. Levo-ketoconazole can increase zidovudine levels by affecting hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 46. Zidovudine and lovotibeglogene autotemcel should not be co-administered. ARTs should be discontinued at least one month before mobilization and until all apheresis cycles are completed. 47. Methadone can increase zidovudine levels by decreasing renal clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 48. Methotrexate and zidovudine can increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, raising the risk of myelosuppression. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 49. Mitomycin and zidovudine can mutually enhance toxicity via pharmacodynamic synergism, increasing the risk of myelosuppression. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 50. Nelfinavir and zidovudine both elevate the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 51. Nevirapine and zidovudine both increase the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 52. Nirmatrelvir can decrease zidovudine levels or effects through an unknown mechanism. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 53. Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir can decrease zidovudine levels or effects through an unknown mechanism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 54. Orlistat can decrease zidovudine levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral form of both agents. Close monitoring of HIV RNA levels is necessary, and orlistat should be discontinued if virological control is lost. 55. Oxaliplatin and zidovudine can increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, heightening the risk of myelosuppression. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 56. Peginterferon alfa-2b can increase zidovudine levels or effects, potentially enhancing adverse effects such as myelosuppression. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 57. Zidovudine can increase the toxicity of pentamidine through pharmacodynamic synergism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 58. Pretomanid can increase zidovudine levels or effects by inhibiting OAT3. Close monitoring for adverse effects is recommended, and dosage adjustments may be necessary. 59. Primaquine and zidovudine can increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, raising the risk of myelosuppression. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 60. Probenecid can increase zidovudine levels by decreasing its metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 61. Zidovudine and pyrimethamine can increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, potentially leading to increased bone marrow toxicity. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 62. Ribavirin can decrease zidovudine effects by competing for thymidine kinase during conversion to its active form. This combination should be avoided or alternative drugs used. 63. Rifabutin can decrease zidovudine levels or effects by affecting hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 64. Rifampin can decrease zidovudine levels by increasing its metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 65. Ritonavir and zidovudine both elevate the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 66. Ropinterferon alfa-2b and zidovudine can increase each other’s toxicity, potentially leading to additive myelosuppression. This combination should be avoided or alternative drugs used. 67. Zidovudine can increase the toxicity of sulfamethoxazole through pharmacodynamic synergism, while sulfamethoxazole can increase zidovudine levels by decreasing renal clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 68. Tenofovir DF and zidovudine both elevate the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 69. Thiotepa and zidovudine can increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, heightening the risk of myelosuppression. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 70. Tipranavir can decrease zidovudine levels through an unspecified mechanism. Both drugs also increase the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 71. Tobramycin inhaled and zidovudine both increase the risk of nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Concurrent or sequential use should be avoided to reduce ototoxicity risk. Close monitoring is necessary. 72. Tocilizumab can decrease zidovudine levels by affecting hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism. This interaction is relevant in inflammatory conditions like rheumatoid arthritis. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 73. Trimethoprim can increase zidovudine levels by decreasing renal clearance, potentially increasing toxicity. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 74. Ublituximab can decrease zidovudine effects through immunosuppressive effects, increasing the risk of infection. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. 75. Vadadustat can increase zidovudine levels or effects by increasing exposure to OAT3 substrates. Close monitoring for adverse effects is necessary, and substrate doses should be adjusted as per product labeling. 76. Valacyclovir can increase zidovudine effects through an unknown mechanism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. Monitoring for lethargy and fatigue is recommended.
